T HERE is a sharp, imperative rap on my outer door; a rap having within its insistent urgency a shadow of delicate diffidence, as though the person responsible were a trifle scared of the performance and on tiptoe to run away. I roll over and regard the clock. Four-forty. One of the dubious by-products of continuous service as a senior assistant at sea is the habit of waking automatically about 4 A. M. This gives one several hours, when ashore, to meditate upon one's sins, frailties, and (more rarely) triumphs and virtues. For a man who gets up at say four-thirty is regarded with aversion ashore. His family express themselves with superfluous vigor. He must lie still and meditate, or suffer the ignominy of being asked when he is going away again.

But this morning, in these old Chambers in an ancient Inn buried in the heart of London City, I have agreed to get up and go out. The reason for this momentous departure from a life of temporary but deliberate indolence is a lady. "Cherchez la femme," as the French say with the dry animosity of a logical race. Well, she is not far to seek, being on the outside of my heavy oak door, tapping, as already hinted, with a sharp insistent delicacy. To this romantic summons I reply with an articulate growl of acquiescence, and proceed to get ready. To relieve the anxiety of any reader who imagines an impending elopement it may be stated in succinct truthfulness that we are bound on no such desperate venture. We are going round the corner a few blocks up the Strand, to Covent Garden Market, to see the arrival of the metropolitan supply of produce.

Having accomplished a hasty toilet, almost as primitive as that favored by gentlemen aroused to go on watch, and placating an occasional repetition of the tapping by brief protests and reports of progress, I take hat and cane, and drawing the huge antique bolts of my door, discover a young woman standing by the window looking out upon the quadrangle of the old Inn. She is a very decided young woman, who is continually thinking out what she calls "stunts" for articles in the press. That is her profession, or one of her professions—writing articles for the press. The other profession is selling manuscripts, which constitutes the tender bond between us. For the usual agent's commission she is selling one of my manuscripts. Being an unattached and, as it were, unprotected male, she plans little excursions about London to keep me instructed and entertained. Here she is attired in the flamboyant finery of a London flowergirl. She is about to get the necessary copy for a special article in a morning paper. With the exception of a certain expectant flash of her bright black Irish eyes, she is entirely businesslike. Commenting on the beauty of an early summer morning in town, we descend, and passing out under the ponderous ancient archway, we make our leisurely progress westward down the Strand.

There comes a distinct, urgent knock at my front door; a knock that carries a hint of nervous hesitation, as if the person outside feels slightly apprehensive about their intrusion and might bolt at any moment. I glance at the clock, which reads four-forty. One of the peculiar habits acquired from my long tenure as a senior assistant at sea is the tendency to wake up around 4 A.M. This oddity grants me several hours, when I’m on land, to reflect on my shortcomings, vices, and, less frequently, my successes and virtues. A man who rises at four-thirty is often met with disdain on shore. Family members express their opinions with exaggerated fervor, insisting he remain still and contemplate or face the embarrassment of inquiries about his next departure.

Yet this morning, in these venerable chambers of a historic inn nestled in the heart of London, I have committed to rising and venturing out. The catalyst for this significant deviation from a life of temporary but conscious leisure is a woman. "Cherchez la femme," as the French express with their trademark logical wit. Fortunately, she is not hard to find, as she stands just outside my solid oak door, tapping with an insistence that is both sharp and delicate. To this romantic call, I respond with a gruff acknowledgment before preparing myself. To ease any concerns from readers imagining an imminent elopement, it should be clearly stated that we are not embarking on any such wild escapade. Instead, we are headed just a few blocks up the Strand to Covent Garden Market to witness the arrival of fresh produce for the city.

After hastily dressing, a routine almost as basic as that of a sailor getting ready for watch, and soothing the occasional repetition of the tapping with brief assurances of my progress, I take my hat and cane. Drawing back the heavy, ornate bolts of my door, I find a young woman looking out the window at the inn's courtyard. She is a decisive character, constantly brainstorming what she terms "stunts" for her articles. This is her profession, or one of them—writing for the press. The other involves selling manuscripts, which creates a special connection between us. For the customary agent's fee, she is representing one of my works. Being an unattached and somewhat unguarded male, she organizes little outings around London to keep me entertained and informed. Today, she is dressed in the vibrant attire of a London flower girl, preparing to gather material for a feature in a morning newspaper. Apart from the eager glint in her bright black Irish eyes, she exudes a sense of professionalism. As we comment on the beauty of an early summer morning in the city, we descend and, passing beneath the imposing ancient archway, we stroll leisurely westward along the Strand.
